stem: Ishaan writes the up-and-down sum $1+2+3+4+3+2+1$ with consecutive counting numbers that climb from $1$ to $4$ and then fall back to $1$.

options.text: The climb from $1$ to $4$ and the fall back to $1$ can be paired to fill a $4$-by-$4$ square of unit tiles.
Any climb-and-fall of whole numbers equals a square, even when the steps are not consecutive counting numbers.
$4^{2}$ is what produces the up-and-down counting sum.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

part_answers.answer: Pairing the climb $1$ to $4$ with the fall $3$ to $1$ fills four rows of length $4$, so the sum is $4^{2}$.

teacher.key_rationale: Consecutive climb-and-fall pairs fill an n-by-n square. Skipping the consecutive condition over-applies the rule. Saying the square produces the sum reverses the relation.
